meta.title: Mohannad Muhana — Software Engineer | Industrial Automation, SCADA & .NET
meta.description: Software engineer building industrial IoT, SCADA and data-acquisition systems end to end — from Modbus and MQTT device integration through ASP.NET Core APIs and SQL/Redis to operator dashboards and production infrastructure. Based in Amman, Jordan.

hero.lede: I design and build the software that carries a measurement from a meter, inverter or PLC all the way to an operator's screen — protocol integration, edge acquisition, ASP.NET Core services, the databases underneath them, and the servers they run on.

about.title: One engineer across the whole signal path
about.p1: I am a software engineer specialising in .NET backend development, industrial IoT, SCADA and real-time data systems. My work sits where software meets physical equipment: designing high-throughput APIs, distributed data-acquisition platforms, industrial communication integrations and the monitoring interfaces engineers actually use.
about.p2: That means I am comfortable at every level of the stack — reading a register map off an inverter, writing the background service that polls it, modelling the time-series table it lands in, exposing it through an authenticated REST API, and configuring the Linux or Windows server that keeps the whole thing online at a remote site.
about.p3: I work alongside electrical, automation and mechanical engineers, which shapes how I build: systems have to survive unreliable links, restarting devices and sites nobody can visit at short notice. I also lead a small development team, including Flutter developers who deliver the mobile side of client projects.

layers.title: Seven layers, one engineer
layers.lede: Most software roles stop at one or two of these. The value I bring is that a problem never has to be handed across a boundary — the device, the protocol, the service, the database, the screen and the server are all mine to reason about.

field.title: Field layer
field.role: The physical equipment a system exists to observe and control. I work from datasheets and register maps to decide what is readable, what is writable, and what a value actually means.

comms.title: Communication layer
comms.role: How measurements physically travel. Choosing between polled and published transport, sizing scan rates, handling timeouts and retries, and reaching sites that have no public address.

edge.title: Edge layer
edge.role: Software that runs at the site itself. Acquisition loops, local buffering so nothing is lost when the uplink fails, protocol translation and forwarding once connectivity returns.

backend.title: Backend layer
backend.role: The services that turn a stream of raw registers into something queryable. Ingestion endpoints, background workers, parallel processing, validation, and the business rules on top.

data.title: Data layer
data.role: Schema design for high-frequency telemetry: time-series tables, retention and aggregation strategy, indexing for range queries, and caching for the values read most often.

app.title: Application layer
app.role: What the operator actually sees. Live status, historical trends, alarm handling with acknowledgement, maintenance workflows and reports — with access scoped by role.

infra.title: Infrastructure layer
infra.role: Where all of it runs. Provisioning servers, deploying applications as supervised services, terminating TLS, configuring DNS and reverse proxies, and making recovery routine.

architecture.title: From field device to cloud
architecture.lede: A real deployment is a chain, and it is only as good as its weakest link. Step through each stage to see what I build there.

device.name: Field devices
device.text: Everything begins with equipment that already exists on site and was not designed with my software in mind. The first engineering task is always the same: establish exactly which registers hold which quantity, in what unit, at what scale, and how often they are worth reading.
doing: Work from vendor datasheets and register maps to build an accurate point list
Determine data types, byte order, scaling factors and engineering units
Set realistic polling intervals for each quantity rather than one global rate
Verify readings against the device display before anything depends on them

protocol.name: Industrial protocols
protocol.text: The transport layer is where most industrial integrations actually fail. Devices share an RS-485 bus, timeouts collide, gateways drop frames, and a link that behaved on the bench behaves differently on a live plant.
doing: Implement Modbus TCP and RTU masters and slaves, and MQTT publish/subscribe
Tune baud rate, parity, response timeouts and delay between polls per bus
Diagnose bus contention and framing errors with purpose-built test tools
Bridge serial-only devices onto the network with serial-to-IP forwarding

edge.name: Edge & datalogger
edge.text: Site connectivity is not guaranteed, so acquisition has to be able to run alone. The edge layer keeps polling and keeps recording whether or not anything upstream is reachable, then reconciles when it is.
doing: Build datalogger services that poll on a schedule and timestamp at the source
Buffer to a local database so an outage costs no data, then forward on recovery
Run acquisition as a supervised background service that survives restarts
Normalise readings from different vendors into one internal representation

service.name: Backend services
service.text: This is where a stream of numbers becomes a system. Ingestion has to keep up with every site at once, which means asynchronous processing, parallelism and back-pressure rather than a request-per-reading design.
doing: Write ingestion endpoints and background workers in ASP.NET Core and Python
Use async processing, multithreading and parallelism for high-throughput loads
Apply validation, derived calculations and business rules on the way in
Cache hot values in Redis so dashboards never hit the historical tables

store.name: Data layer
store.text: High-frequency telemetry punishes naive schemas quickly. The storage design decides whether a year of history stays queryable or becomes something nobody dares to open.
doing: Design schemas for high-frequency time-series, configuration and reporting
Index and optimise queries for range scans over long historical windows
Separate live state, historical records and configuration into distinct concerns
Use Redis for current values, counters and expensive intermediate results

api.name: Cloud API
api.text: Once data is stored it has to be reachable — by dashboards, by mobile apps, by other companies' systems — without exposing the database or every site's internals to whoever asks.
doing: Build documented REST APIs with Swagger/OpenAPI contracts
Secure them with JWT and OAuth2, scoped by role-based authorisation
Expose discovery, query and telemetry endpoints across multiple projects
Version and shape responses so client applications are not tied to the schema

ui.name: SCADA & dashboards
ui.text: The last stage is the only one most people ever see. An operator interface has to answer 'is it running, and if not, why' in seconds — not present a beautiful chart of something nobody asked about.
doing: Build Angular and web front-ends for live status, trends and equipment detail
Deliver alarm consoles with acknowledgement, priority and event history
Push live updates over SignalR/WebSockets instead of polling from the browser
Scope every view and control action to the signed-in user's role

projects.title: Systems in production
projects.lede: Grouped by the engineering system they form rather than by repository. Several are internal industrial software whose interfaces cannot be published — those are shown as architecture diagrams.

israr-cloud.title: Israr Cloud Platform
israr-cloud.tagline: A centralised ASP.NET Core platform that makes historical data from many separate industrial projects reachable through one authenticated API and one web client.
israr-cloud.overview: Industrial projects tend to accumulate as islands: each site ends up with its own database, its own table naming and its own way of being queried. This platform puts a single addressable layer over all of them, so a dashboard, a report or an external system can ask for data without knowing which project it lives in or how that project happens to be structured.
israr-cloud.problem: Every new site meant another database with a different schema, and every new client application meant writing bespoke query code against it. Onboarding a project was a development task rather than a configuration task, and nothing could be queried across sites.
israr-cloud.solution: I built an ASP.NET Core Web API that discovers the projects and tables available to it at runtime instead of hard-coding them, and exposes their historical and live data through a consistent, documented set of endpoints. Access is authenticated with JWT and scoped per role, MySQL holds the data, Redis caches the values requested most often, and an Angular client consumes the same public API as any other consumer.
features: Dynamic project and table discovery, so a new site is configured rather than coded
Consistent query endpoints for historical, aggregated and latest-value data
JWT authentication with role-based authorisation over projects and endpoints
Telemetry ingestion endpoints shared by dataloggers and edge services
Redis caching for frequently requested values and expensive aggregations
Angular front-end built against the same documented API as external consumers
challenges: Keeping a generic query layer efficient — a discovery-driven API can easily produce queries that a purpose-built one would never issue
Designing one response shape flexible enough for differing project schemas without becoming untyped and unusable
Enforcing authorisation across projects that were never designed with a shared permission model
Keeping response times acceptable for long historical ranges as sites accumulate
role: Designed the platform architecture and the API contract
Implemented the ASP.NET Core services, discovery layer and authentication
Modelled and optimised the MySQL schema and its query paths
Integrated the Angular client and supported other consuming applications
capabilities: One integration point for every industrial project
New sites onboarded without new API code
Authenticated, role-scoped access to historical data

datalogger.title: Industrial Data Acquisition & Synchronisation Platform
datalogger.tagline: The acquisition backbone: edge dataloggers, local buffering, synchronisation services and format converters that move plant data from field devices to central databases without losing records.
datalogger.overview: This is one platform made of several cooperating services rather than a single application — acquisition at the edge, local persistence, synchronisation to the centre, and the conversion utilities that bridge legacy formats. Together they handle a distributed multi-site workload processing over 60,000 data points per minute across more than ten industrial sites.
datalogger.problem: Remote industrial sites do not have reliable connectivity. An acquisition design that writes straight to a central database loses everything the moment a link drops — and on a plant, gaps in historical data are not a cosmetic problem: they invalidate performance reporting and availability figures.
datalogger.solution: I built acquisition as an edge-first system. Dataloggers poll devices on a fixed cycle and timestamp at the source, writing to a local database so the site keeps recording regardless of the uplink. Separate synchronisation services reconcile local records with the central database once connectivity returns, deduplicating rather than overwriting. Parallel processing, caching and resilient retry handling let the central side absorb every site at once, and converters translate between XML and database representations where legacy equipment requires it.
features: Scheduled polling of Modbus TCP/RTU and MQTT devices with source timestamping
Local buffering (MySQL and SQLite variants) so link outages cost no data
Synchronisation services that reconcile and deduplicate on reconnection
Parallel processing and caching to absorb concurrent load from every site
XML and database format conversion for legacy equipment and exports
A simulator for developing and testing without occupying real plant hardware
challenges: Sustaining a very high aggregate ingestion rate without falling behind the poll cycle
Making synchronisation idempotent, so a retried batch never duplicates history
Reconciling clock differences between edge devices and the central system
Detecting a stalled device — one that answers but returns stale values — not just a disconnected one
Keeping memory and disk bounded on edge hardware during a long outage
role: Designed the edge-first acquisition and synchronisation architecture
Implemented the datalogger services, buffering and forwarding logic
Built the synchronisation, conversion and simulation components
Tuned database schemas and the ingestion path for sustained throughput
capabilities: 60,000+ data points per minute across the platform
10+ industrial sites synchronised centrally
Continuous recording through connectivity outages

ppc.title: Power Plant Controller & Solar Plant Integration
ppc.tagline: Plant-level control software for solar sites: reading grid metering, computing setpoints, distributing them to inverters, and feeding the resulting telemetry back into SCADA.
ppc.overview: A power plant controller sits between the grid connection point and the inverters, holding the plant to whatever the grid operator requires. It is a closed loop with a hard real-time character — measure at the point of common coupling, compute, command, verify, repeat — running continuously and unattended.
ppc.problem: Solar plants must respect active power limits and operating conditions imposed at the grid connection point, but the inverters producing that power are individually addressed devices with their own communication behaviour. Something has to translate a plant-level requirement into per-device commands and confirm they took effect.
ppc.solution: I developed the controller service in C#/.NET as a continuously running background service. It reads power meters and inverters over Modbus TCP, computes plant-level setpoints from measured conditions, distributes commands across the inverter fleet, and reads status back to verify each command was applied. Every cycle — measurements, computed values, commands and device responses — is recorded for telemetry and performance analysis, and the same data feeds the SCADA layer.
features: Continuous measurement of grid meters and inverters over Modbus TCP
Active power management: plant setpoints distributed across the inverter fleet
Command verification through status readback rather than fire-and-forget writes
Performance and availability calculations from measured plant data
Telemetry recorded per control cycle for analysis and reporting
Integration with SCADA for plant status, trends and operator visibility
challenges: Maintaining a stable control loop when device response times vary across the fleet
Handling inverters that drop off mid-cycle without destabilising the plant setpoint
Keeping computation deterministic and bounded so a cycle never overruns its period
Distinguishing a device that rejected a command from one that never received it
role: Developed the controller service and its control-cycle logic
Implemented inverter and meter communication over Modbus TCP
Designed the telemetry and performance-calculation data model
Integrated plant data with the SCADA and monitoring layer
capabilities: Plant-level active power management
Verified command delivery to the inverter fleet
Continuous performance telemetry for the site

alarm-engine.title: Industrial Alarm & Event Management Engine
alarm-engine.tagline: A real-time alarm backend with configurable rules, full event lifecycle tracking, acknowledgement and history — delivering equipment and process alarms to SCADA and web dashboards.
alarm-engine.overview: Alarming is deceptively hard: the mechanical part — comparing a value to a threshold — is trivial, and everything that makes an alarm system usable is the part around it. State transitions, acknowledgement, priority, suppression of chatter, and a history that can be audited afterwards. This engine handles that lifecycle for equipment and process alarms across the plant.
alarm-engine.problem: Alarm behaviour was effectively fixed: changing what constituted an alarm meant changing code, there was no consistent record of who acknowledged what and when, and an operator facing a genuine fault could be buried under repeated notifications from a single flapping signal.
alarm-engine.solution: I built an ASP.NET Core backend that evaluates configurable rules against incoming tag values and drives each alarm through an explicit state machine — raised, active, acknowledged, cleared — rather than treating alarms as instantaneous notifications. Every transition is persisted as an event with its timestamp and originating condition, giving a complete audit history. Live alarm state is pushed to SCADA and web dashboards through real-time channels, and priority determines what an operator sees first. In production this reduced operational issue response time by roughly 40%.
features: Alarm rules configured at runtime instead of compiled into the application
Explicit lifecycle: raised, active, acknowledged and cleared states
Operator acknowledgement recorded with user and timestamp
Priority levels so a genuine fault is not buried under routine warnings
Complete historical event record for auditing and post-incident review
Real-time delivery to SCADA and web dashboards, plus REST access to history
challenges: Suppressing chatter from a signal oscillating around its threshold without hiding a real fault
Guaranteeing no alarm is lost or duplicated when a client reconnects mid-event
Evaluating rules across many tags fast enough to stay genuinely real-time
Modelling event history so long-running alarms and their acknowledgements stay reconstructable
role: Designed the alarm state machine and event data model
Implemented the rule evaluation engine and configuration layer
Built the REST and real-time delivery channels to SCADA and web clients
Tuned evaluation and storage for sustained tag throughput
capabilities: Operational response time improved by approximately 40%
Auditable history of every alarm and acknowledgement
Alarm behaviour reconfigurable without a deployment

solar-tracker.title: Solar Tracker Controller
solar-tracker.tagline: Control and monitoring software for solar tracking systems — solar position computation, backtracking, per-tracker positioning over RS-485, and live status across a zone of trackers.
solar-tracker.overview: A tracking array only pays for itself if every tracker is actually where it should be. This application manages a hierarchy of project, zone, gateway, serial port and individual tracker, computes where each one ought to point from solar geometry, issues positioning commands over Modbus RTU, and shows the resulting angles and alarms for the whole zone at once.
solar-tracker.problem: Trackers are individually addressed devices on shared RS-485 buses, and their correct target angle is not a fixed value — it depends on time, date, site latitude and longitude, array geometry and whether neighbouring rows would shade each other. Commissioning and operating them by hand does not scale past a handful of units.
solar-tracker.solution: I developed a C#/.NET application that computes solar position and derives the correct tracker angle, including backtracking to avoid row-to-row shading at low sun elevations. Results are cross-checked against the NREL solar position algorithm. The tool addresses trackers through a configurable project/zone/gateway/port hierarchy over Modbus RTU on RS-485, supports manual, automatic-local, automatic-remote, calibration, programming, emergency and parking modes, and monitors angle feedback, limit switches, wind conditions and digital I/O with an acknowledgeable alarm list.

Cross-checked against the NREL solar position algorithm
Project → zone → gateway → serial port → tracker configuration hierarchy
Modbus RTU addressing over RS-485 with configurable serial parameters
Operating modes: manual, auto-local, auto-remote, calibration, programming, emergency and parking
Live monitoring of target vs. current angle, limit switches and digital I/O
Wind speed limits with configurable timeouts for protective positioning
NTP and RTC time synchronisation across plant, gateway and tracker
Alarm list with acknowledgement covering communication, position, movement and data validation
challenges: Getting solar geometry right — an error of a degree is invisible in testing and costly in yield
Implementing backtracking so rows stop shading each other at low sun angles
Sharing one RS-485 bus across many trackers without response collisions

protocol-toolkit.title: Industrial Protocol & Device Integration Toolkit
protocol-toolkit.tagline: The diagnostic tools commissioning actually depends on: a Modbus master, a Modbus slave simulator and a serial-to-IP port forwarder, used to prove a link before anything is built on top of it.
protocol-toolkit.overview: Before a datalogger or a controller can be trusted, someone has to establish that the device really answers, that the register you think holds active power actually does, and that the bus stays stable under continuous polling. These tools exist to answer those questions on site, quickly, without a debugger attached to production software.
protocol-toolkit.problem: When an integration fails on a live plant, the failure is ambiguous: it might be the cabling, the serial parameters, the slave address, the function code, the register offset, the byte order, or the application. General-purpose utilities do not carry the site's register naming and scaling, so every diagnosis restarts from raw numbers.
protocol-toolkit.solution: I built a set of C#/.NET engineering tools that isolate each layer. The Modbus master polls multiple devices simultaneously in separate monitoring windows, each with its own slave ID, function code, address range and scan rate, showing raw, ordered and scaled values side by side along with live Tx/Rx counters and per-transaction frames. The slave simulator presents a configurable device so the other side of an integration can be developed and tested without hardware present. The port forwarder bridges serial devices to the network, letting a physically remote device be reached as though it were local.
features: Modbus master over TCP and RTU, with several devices polled concurrently
Per-window slave ID, function code, start address, quantity and scan rate
Raw, byte-ordered and engineering-scaled values displayed together
Live Tx/Rx counters and per-transaction frame inspection for diagnosis
Read and write function support for testing commands, not just reads
Modbus slave simulator for developing against a device that is not present
Serial-to-IP port forwarder with independent source and destination settings
Configurable serial parameters: baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, flow control
Named register maps saved per device so diagnosis starts from meaning, not offsets
challenges: Presenting byte order and scaling clearly enough that a wrong reading is obvious at a glance
Polling several devices concurrently without the UI thread stalling on a slow response
Making timeout and inter-poll delay behaviour explicit, since these cause most field failures

Implemented the Modbus TCP and RTU communication layers

Integrations developed before hardware is available

device-configurator.title: Device Configuration & Commissioning Suite
device-configurator.tagline: One tool to configure an entire hardware product family — interfaces, protocol stacks, I/O expansion and RTC — write it to the device over USB or Ethernet, and generate the matching firmware project.
device-configurator.overview: A hardware product line accumulates variants: different microcontroller boards, different fitted options, different protocol requirements per customer. This application holds the whole device database in one place, so configuring a unit is a structured task against a known model rather than a hand-edited settings file.
device-configurator.problem: Every device variant had its own combination of fitted hardware, enabled interfaces and supported protocols. Without a single tool, commissioning meant remembering which options a given board actually had, editing configuration by hand, and rediscovering the correct values on the next unit.
device-configurator.solution: I built a C#/.NET configurator organised around a device database, with each device broken into communication, protocols, monitoring, calibration and general-purpose sections. It configures Ethernet and RS-485 serial interfaces independently, selects which protocol stacks each interface exposes, manages I²C extension boards and their I/O expanders, and handles RTC synchronisation against PC time. Configuration is written to the device over USB virtual COM or HTTP, live register and bit-level I/O state can be read back to verify the result, and the tool generates matching Arduino or PlatformIO firmware projects from the configured device definition.

breaker-control.title: Remote Breaker Control & Switchgear Interface
breaker-control.tagline: Remote operation of switchgear with validated commands, verified status readback and a full audit trail — for equipment on sites that cannot be attended at short notice.
breaker-control.overview: Remote control of switchgear is one of the few places where industrial software can cause a physical consequence. That shapes every design decision: a command is not simply sent, it is validated against current state, confirmed against readback, and recorded so it is always clear what was operated, when, and by whom.
breaker-control.problem: Operating a breaker required someone on site. But an unconditional remote write is not an acceptable alternative — a command issued against stale state, or one that silently fails, is worse than no remote control at all.
breaker-control.solution: I built a control service that treats every operation as a transaction. The request is validated against the equipment's current reported state before anything is written, the command is issued over Modbus TCP across the site link, and the resulting state is read back and compared against what was intended. Communication health is monitored continuously so operations are refused rather than attempted over a degraded link, and every request, outcome and originating user is persisted as an audit record.
features: Validated commands checked against current equipment state before dispatch
Status readback and comparison to confirm the operation actually took effect
Continuous communication monitoring, with commands refused on a degraded link
Full audit trail: who requested what, when, and what the device reported
Modbus TCP integration with switchgear over VPN-connected site networks
Clear separation between a failed command and an unconfirmed one
challenges: Guaranteeing a command is never applied twice when a response is lost in transit
Deciding what a timeout means when the operation may or may not have completed
Keeping reported state current enough that validation is meaningful, not decorative
Failing safe: refusing operation is always preferable to acting on stale information

api-integrations.title: External System & Vendor API Integrations
api-integrations.tagline: Integration services that pull data from vendor cloud platforms and third-party systems into internal databases and APIs on a reliable schedule.
api-integrations.overview: Not every measurement comes off a device we own. Equipment vendors expose their own cloud platforms, partners publish their own APIs, and each does it differently — different authentication, different rate limits, different units, different ideas of what a timestamp means. These services absorb that variation so the rest of the platform sees one consistent shape.
api-integrations.problem: Each external integration written directly against its provider became a separate small system with its own failure modes. When a token expired or a provider rate-limited a request, the failure surfaced somewhere unrelated and often silently.
api-integrations.solution: I built integration clients in Python and C# that share a common structure: authentication and token refresh handled in one place, scheduled retrieval rather than on-demand fetching, normalisation into internal units and naming conventions, and persistence into the internal database. FastAPI services expose the results downstream, so consumers depend on our contract rather than the vendor's. Failures are contained to their own integration and logged where they can actually be seen.

challenges: Respecting rate limits while still keeping data current enough to be useful

cmms.title: CMMS — Maintenance & Asset Management Platform
cmms.tagline: A web platform for industrial asset management: equipment registers, maintenance planning, work orders and equipment history, with access scoped by role.
cmms.overview: Monitoring tells you what equipment is doing now; a CMMS tells you what has been done to it and what is due. This platform holds the asset register, the maintenance plans built on it, and the work orders those plans generate — so maintenance history lives with the equipment rather than in someone's spreadsheet.
cmms.problem: Maintenance activity was recorded separately from the equipment it applied to. Scheduled work depended on individual memory, and when a machine failed there was no straightforward way to see what had recently been done to it.
cmms.solution: I built an ASP.NET Core web platform around a structured asset register, with maintenance plans attached to equipment and work orders generated from them. Technicians record completion against the work order, which accumulates into per-equipment history. Role-based access separates what an operator, a technician and a supervisor can each see and do, and reporting views summarise outstanding and completed work.
features: Structured equipment and asset register
Maintenance plans and schedules attached to specific equipment
Work order creation, assignment and completion tracking

cowrmat.title: COWRMAT — Crop Optimisation & Water Reuse Allocation
cowrmat.tagline: A decision-support platform that models crop water demand from evapotranspiration data and treated wastewater availability, so allocation decisions can be compared as scenarios rather than estimated.
cowrmat.overview: COWRMAT helps plan which crops to grow, and how to allocate treated wastewater to them, using an established agronomic water-balance method rather than rules of thumb. A user selects crops, planting dates and a treatment plant, and the platform computes the monthly water demand that follows — with results exportable and comparable across scenarios.
cowrmat.problem: Allocating treated wastewater to agriculture involves crop water demand that changes month by month with the crop, its growth stage and local climate. Doing that by hand for several crops across several treatment plants is slow and hard to revisit, so decisions tend to rely on approximations that cannot easily be compared.
cowrmat.solution: I built a web platform that computes reference evapotranspiration (ETo), applies crop coefficients (Kc) per crop and month, and derives crop evapotranspiration (ETc) as the basis for water demand — the standard FAO-56 approach. Treatment plant flow data is imported from CSV, irrigation efficiency is applied as a configurable factor, and results are presented as monthly tables and charts exportable to Excel and PDF. An administrative dashboard tracks usage across users, plants and crop combinations, and access is separated by role.

ecommerce.title: E-Commerce Platform
ecommerce.tagline: A full online store built on ASP.NET Core: product catalogue, cart, payment integration and order tracking, with an admin side for the people running it.
ecommerce.overview: A complete storefront and the back office behind it. Customers browse a catalogue, build a cart and pay; staff manage products, stock and orders from an admin dashboard. The interesting engineering is not the shop front — it is keeping catalogue, stock and orders consistent while payment happens on someone else's server.
ecommerce.problem: A store is only useful if its state stays correct under concurrency. Two customers can reach the last item at the same moment, a payment can succeed while the browser never comes back, and a provider can confirm a charge minutes after the request. Handling those honestly is what separates a working store from a demo.
ecommerce.solution: I built the platform on ASP.NET Core with MySQL, structured around the order as explicit state rather than a flag on a row. An order moves through pending, paid, fulfilled and cancelled, and the payment provider's confirmation — not the browser's return trip — is what advances it. Stock is decremented against a reservation so a cart cannot oversell, and Redis caches catalogue reads so browsing never contends with checkout.

hotel.title: Hotel Reservation & Booking Platform
hotel.tagline: A reservation system with a live availability calendar, online payment, automated confirmations and an admin dashboard for rooms, rates and guests.
hotel.overview: Booking is a scheduling problem wearing a web interface. A room is not a quantity in stock, it is a resource occupied over a date range, and the whole system follows from modelling that correctly. Guests search dates and pay; staff manage rooms, rates, arrivals and guest records.
hotel.problem: Availability cannot be answered by counting rows. A room is free for a requested stay only if no existing reservation overlaps it, and two guests searching the same dates at the same moment must not both be able to confirm. Getting that wrong produces double bookings, which cost far more to resolve than to prevent.
hotel.solution: I modelled reservations as date intervals against a room and resolved availability by overlap rather than by a count, so the calendar is derived from the reservations themselves and cannot drift out of sync with them. Confirmation is guarded so a room cannot be committed twice for overlapping dates. Payment goes through an external provider, confirmations are sent automatically on state changes, and staff work from an admin dashboard covering rooms, rates, arrivals and guests.
